The farming peoples of western Europe who raised monuments of huge stones in the Neolithic and Bronze Ages. The tradition began well before this chart's start, around 4500 BCE, and was strongest along the Atlantic coasts, from Portugal and Brittany to Ireland, Britain and Scandinavia. More than 35,000 megalithic structures are known in Europe.

They had no writing and no states that we know of. They were communities of farmers and herders who could still gather the labour of many people over many years.

Their best-known works:

  • Newgrange, in Ireland, a great passage tomb built around 3200 BCE. At the winter solstice, the rising sun shines down its passage to the inner chamber.
  • Stonehenge, in England, built in stages from about 3000 BCE to about 1500 BCE. Some of its stones were dragged from Wales, more than 200 km away.
  • The Carnac stones in Brittany, thousands of standing stones set in long rows.

Other forms include dolmens, simple tombs of upright stones topped by a slab, and stone circles.

What they were for is partly guessed. Many were tombs or places for the dead; many are lined up with the sun, so they likely marked seasons and festivals. They show that early farmers shared ideas over long distances by sea.

Around 2500 BCE new people arrived in Britain and western Europe with the Bell Beaker culture, bringing metal and ancestry from the steppe. The building of new great monuments slowly ended in the Bronze Age, while the old ones stayed in use and in legend. Further east, the Minoans were by then building palaces.
